entries.test: Enterprise deployment studies, employment records, and documented implementation failures would show whether generative AI changes businesses, replaces workers, and impedes adoption through technical failures.
entries.note: The proposition narrows 'anything' to businesses and omits his later qualification that worker replacement means at scale. The adoption explanation is causal.

entries.test: AI companies' financial disclosures and enterprise revenue and profitability would show whether enterprise demand makes their businesses financially sustainable.
entries.note: The plain reading of 'save' is financial rescue through enterprise demand; no deadline is given.

entries.test: Public enterprise product evaluations and user studies would show whether the tools deliver their promised functionality and whether users recognize failures.
entries.note: The immediate context concerns enterprise tools in the cited study; the normalization generalizes to generative AI products overall.
There is no shared operational definition of 'intellect' or 'intelligent' here. The accompanying characterization also concerns promoters' dispositions and motives.

entries.test: Reliability evaluations, resource-use measurements, financial results, and controlled user studies would test the asserted inconsistency, inefficiency, financial losses, and added cognitive load.
entries.note: The passage contains evaluative language but also concrete empirical assertions.

entries.test: Reproducible demonstrations of AI agents successfully completing their intended tasks would test the categorical claim that they do not work at all.
entries.note: His subsequent discussion emphasizes autonomous job performance, but the quoted assertion is categorical.

entries.test: Documented deployments in which agents autonomously perform jobs or replace coders would test the prediction.
entries.note: The passage combines present observations, a causal explanation, and an undated prediction.
He says 'will likely.' The normalization also labels the entire spending total as AI spending, although the quoted baseline is total big-tech capital expenditure.
He discusses exposure, elapsed time, and resources, but supplies no common threshold separating early from later days.

entries.test: Public evidence of widely adopted AI products performing identifiable practical tasks, alongside funding records, would test the claim.
entries.note: A defined practical use with mass-market adoption provides a plain test despite the adjective 'meaningful'.
Neither the end of the 'LLM era' nor what counts as nearing it is defined.

entries.test: Following an AI investment collapse, bankruptcy records for major GPU buyers would show whether most survive.
entries.note: The source predicts buyers' survival; it does not explicitly predict that their GPUs will not flood the market.

entries.test: Documented widespread deployment of AI GPUs for another application would test the prediction that no other mass-scale use will emerge.
entries.note: The technical explanation is separately testable using GPU architecture and performance evidence.

entries.test: Public GPU inventory, utilization, resale, and deployment records would show whether substantial purchased capacity sits unused awaiting applications.
entries.note: The normalization converts 'not an infrastructure buildout' into 'not useful infrastructure' and broadens the denial of an enduring alternative use case.

entries.test: A publicly documented and independently evaluated agent demonstrating the autonomous self-learning capabilities assumed in AI 2027 would test the prediction.
entries.note: The target is the scenario's self-learning agent, not every system that updates from data.
Calling the scenario 'fan fiction' and its authors grifters is a dismissal without a defined forecasting-performance claim.

entries.test: Published model evaluations and ablation studies would show whether any capability improvements came from methods other than additional reasoning tokens.
entries.note: The word 'only' makes this an empirical exclusivity claim.

entries.test: Historical application-level inference bills and token consumption for comparable workloads would show whether inference costs rose over the period discussed.
entries.note: His supporting argument concerns total application costs, although he also discusses providers' underlying serving costs.
The future possibility is explicitly 'maybe'; the firm commitment concerns the existing cost trend. That historical component could be checked separately.

entries.test: A dated body of mainstream media reporting would show whether coverage shifts noticeably toward recognizing rising application inference costs.
entries.note: 'I predict' expresses a firm expectation, with no deadline.

entries.test: Reproducible reliability studies and architectural analyses would show whether LLMs systematically produce errors and inconsistent outputs attributable to their design.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion gives 'unreliable' a practical meaning involving erroneous or inconsistent outputs.

entries.test: Successive model releases' disclosed sizes and training or serving costs would establish whether the stated upward trend existed at publication.
entries.note: This describes an existing trend rather than a dated future outcome.

entries.test: Scaling studies, model ablations, and application cost breakdowns would test whether diminishing training returns forced token-intensive reasoning and thereby increased inference costs.
entries.note: The claim includes the strong assertion that no other improvement route was available.

entries.test: Public demonstrations of improved model capabilities without increased reasoning-token consumption would test whether developers can escape the asserted path.
entries.note: In context, 'out of ideas' supports a concrete prediction about the available route to improvement.

entries.test: After substantial government customization spending, public audits and operational records would show whether government services materially depend on ChatGPT.
entries.note: The surrounding comparison with taxis gives 'essential' the practical meaning of operational dependence.

entries.test: Public deployment evidence and comparisons with available substitutes would show whether any generative AI use produces dependence comparable to urban taxi services.
entries.note: The source uses a specific comparison with cabs; the normalization replaces it with an unqualified claim about essentiality.

entries.test: Economic impact studies separating construction spending from continuing operations would measure AI data centers' contribution to growth.
entries.note: The relevant comparison is ongoing economic activity versus the construction boom.
'Maybe $40 billion' is more tentative than an asserted approximate total. The no-profit component is firm and independently checkable.

entries.test: Operating data centers' employment records, local economic studies, utility consumption, land records, and environmental monitoring would test these assertions.
entries.note: 'Once built' identifies the operating phase; it does not make this a future forecast.

entries.test: Uber's cumulative losses and the stated allocations of partner capex and AI-company funding would establish whether each calculated total exceeds four times Uber's burn.
entries.note: The surrounding text explicitly counts partner infrastructure. Checkability does not validate treating funding or allocated capex as cash burn.

entries.test: Microsoft's reported and projected capex and OpenAI's funding announcements would allow reproduction of the stated 30%-plus-funding calculation.
entries.note: This tests his stipulated accounting calculation, not whether 30% is the actual attributable share.

entries.test: Amazon's reported and projected capex and Anthropic's funding announcements would allow reproduction of the stated 30%-plus-funding calculation.
entries.note: The attribution percentage is an assumption, not a demonstrated allocation.
He says 'a good chance.' The normalization also narrows total Amazon and Microsoft capex to AI capex.

entries.test: Public controlled demonstrations of LLMs learning new information and revising conclusions would test the categorical inability claim.
entries.note: The source denies the abilities themselves; 'the way humans do' adds a narrower requirement about how they are performed.
Public evidence can assess arguments for AGI's feasibility, but cannot establish that every person claiming knowledge knowingly lies.

entries.test: Archived marketing and reporting compared with documented product capabilities would show whether the promoted implications were misleading.
entries.note: His later examples explain 'lies of inference' as misleading impressions about capabilities.

entries.test: METR's published methodology and interaction records would establish which TaskRabbit actions were performed by researchers and which were generated or executed by GPT-4.
entries.note: The normalization captures his factual interpretation without retaining his speculation about undisclosed prompts.
This is a recommendation about OpenAI's responsibility to correct reporting.

entries.test: Independent evaluations of ChatGPT agent completing complex multistep tasks would test the categorical denial of its advertised capability.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion grounds 'powerful' in practical complex-task performance.
This attributes a private reporting motive. The normalization also turns his belief about higher monthly users into an unqualified fact.
The monthly-user estimate is explicitly 'likely' and a guess. The weekly conversion arithmetic can be checked separately.

entries.test: OpenAI's revenue growth series and public customer-retention and return-on-investment evidence would show whether growth slows because business customers fail to obtain returns.
entries.note: The prediction includes a causal explanation and no deadline.

entries.test: Contemporaneous comparisons of ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok's capabilities, prices, and supported tasks would test their asserted practical equivalence.
entries.note: The preceding sentence defines the comparison in terms of quality, cost, and functionality.

entries.test: Training scaling results and evidence of infrastructure-enabled capability or cost advantages would test whether diminishing returns leave OpenAI only a serving-scale advantage.
entries.note: The proposition explicitly derives the limitation on infrastructure benefits from diminishing training returns.

entries.test: OpenAI's subsequent revenue and paid-to-active-user ratios would show whether growth persists and whether conversion improves materially in the near term.
entries.note: 'I don't buy' is weaker than a categorical denial of indefinite growth, while 'won't change' is broader than 'won't improve.' More than a year has elapsed for the near-term conversion claim.

entries.test: Research and employment evidence available at publication would show whether a causal link between AI adoption and young people's job-finding difficulties had been established.
entries.note: This concerns the available evidence in August 2025, not whether AI could ever affect youth employment.

entries.test: Employment data and documented employer substitution of AI for junior coding positions would show whether such replacement was occurring at scale at publication.
entries.note: The following paragraph explicitly supplies the 'at scale' qualification.

entries.test: Independently validated scientific research conducted by foundation models would test the prediction that they will not do scientific research.
entries.note: The rejection is Zitron's own assertion, despite appearing beside a booster quip.
The claim is expressly limited to what he has personally seen and recognized as transformative.

entries.test: Independent end-to-end software development evaluations would show whether AI can produce working software without a person supplying coding expertise.
entries.note: The surrounding passage distinguishes autonomous software creation from assisting someone who can code.

entries.test: A documented app built entirely by a noncoder using AI, with independent functionality and security validation, would test the impossibility claim.
entries.note: The preceding paragraph supplies the concrete requirements for the app.

entries.test: Controlled studies comparing developers' completion times with and without AI coding environments would test the asserted absence of productivity gains.
entries.note: He answers his own question with an endorsed negative judgment and cites an empirical study.

entries.test: Documented independently validated examples of noncoders producing functional, secure, useful applications entirely through vibe coding would test the prediction.
entries.note: The surrounding paragraphs define what he means by vibe coding working; no future deadline is specified.
The source withholds a claim that the bubble is 'bursting'; the normalization only withholds a claim that it 'has burst.' 'Things begin to collapse' has no shared sector-wide test here.
